content: The solution is isotonic with a pH of 7 and does not contain chlorofluorocarbons. Each unit contains 5 mg of nicotine. The droplets produced by the device are larger than 8 microns in size. A single nicotine nasal spray unit provides approximately 200 applications. Pharmacodynamics Nicotine exerts cardiovascular effects, including peripheral vasoconstriction, tachycardia, and increased blood pressure. Both acute and chronic tolerance to nicotine can develop through smoking or the use of nicotine preparations. Acute tolerance, defined as a reduced response to a given dose, develops rapidly (within less than one hour), but the rate of tolerance development varies depending on the physiological effect (e.g., skin temperature, heart rate, subjective effects). Withdrawal symptoms, such as cigarette cravings, can be alleviated in most individuals by maintaining plasma nicotine levels lower than those achieved through smoking. Withdrawal from nicotine in addicted individuals is characterized by symptoms such as craving, nervousness, restlessness, irritability, mood swings, anxiety, drowsiness, sleep disturbances, impaired concentration, increased appetite, minor somatic complaints (e.g., headache, muscle pain, constipation, fatigue), and weight gain. Nicotine toxicity manifests as nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, flushing, dizziness, disturbances in hearing and vision, confusion, weakness, palpitations, altered respiration, and hypotension. Both smoking and nicotine use can elevate circulating cortisol and catecholamine levels. Notably, tolerance does not develop to the catecholamine-releasing effects of nicotine. Dosage and Absorption One dose of nicotine nasal spray is defined as 1 mg of nicotine, delivered via two sprays (one in each nostril). Following administration of two sprays, approximately 53% ± 16% (mean ± SD) of the nicotine enters systemic circulation. The rate and extent of absorption are not significantly affected by the deposition of nicotine on different parts of the nasal mucosa. Plasma nicotine concentrations from a single 1 mg dose rise rapidly, reaching peak venous concentrations of 2–12 ng/mL within 4–15 minutes. The apparent absorption half-life of nicotine is approximately 3 minutes. There is significant interindividual variability in plasma nicotine concentrations achieved with the spray. Approximately 20% of individuals reach peak nicotine concentrations similar to those observed after smoking one cigarette (7–17 ng/mL). Distribution The volume of distribution of nicotine following intravenous administration is approximately 2–3 L/kg. Plasma protein binding of nicotine is less than 5%, meaning that changes in plasma protein levels due to concomitant drug use or disease states are unlikely to significantly affect nicotine kinetics. Metabolism Nicotine undergoes extensive metabolism, with more than 20 metabolites identified, all of which are less active than the parent compound. The primary urinary metabolites are cotinine (15% of the dose) and trans-3-hydroxycotinine (45% of the dose). Cotinine has a half-life of 15–20 hours and is present at concentrations 10 times higher than nicotine. The liver is the primary site of nicotine metabolism, with the kidney and lung also contributing. Elimination Approximately 10% of absorbed nicotine is excreted unchanged in the urine. This percentage can increase to up to 30% with high urine flow rates and urinary acidification below pH 5. The apparent elimination half-life of nicotine from the nasal spray is 1–2 hours. Pharmacokinetic Model The pharmacokinetic data are well described by a two-compartment model with first-order input. The apparent clearance is approximately 82 L/kg in adults weighing 76 ± 15 kg. Gender Differences Interindividual variability in pharmacokinetic parameters (AUC, Cmax, and clearance/kg) is approximately 50% for both genders. No significant differences in nicotine nasal spray kinetics were observed between males and females. Drug-Drug Interactions The extent of nicotine absorption is slightly reduced (by approximately 10%) in patients with the common cold or rhinitis. The time to peak plasma concentration is prolonged by approximately 30% (delayed by 7 minutes on average). The use of a nasal vasoconstrictor, such as xylometazoline, in patients with rhinitis further prolongs the time to peak concentration by approximately 40% (delayed by 15 minutes on average), although the peak plasma concentration remains unchanged. Nonclinical Toxicology Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and Impairment of Fertility Nicotine itself does not appear to be carcinogenic in laboratory animals. However, nicotine and its metabolites have been shown to increase tumor incidence in the cheek pouches of hamsters and the forestomach of F344 rats when combined with tumor initiators. One study, which could not be replicated, suggested that cotinine, the primary metabolite of nicotine, may cause lymphoreticular sarcoma in the large intestine of rats. Neither nicotine nor cotinine was mutagenic in the Ames Salmonella test. Nicotine induced repairable DNA damage in an E. coli test system and was shown to be genotoxic in a test system using Chinese hamster ovary cells. In rats and rabbits, nicotine can delay or inhibit implantation by reducing DNA synthesis. Studies have also shown a decrease in litter size in rats treated with nicotine during gestation. Clinical Studies The efficacy of nicotine nasal spray therapy as an aid to smoking cessation was demonstrated in three single-center, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials involving a total of 730 patients.
